330.title: The first mountain, from the top
330.hook: the whole year in one sitting
330.tomorrow: Year one close: the big lookout
330.howItsDone: Many Buddhists mark the end of a retreat or a year of practice by reflecting on what they have learned, rejoicing in the good done (mudita), and dedicating it to others before beginning again.

segments.voice: Yesterday: looking back at the depths, and your line, there's more. Did you name one room you'd like to come back to someday? Day three hundred thirty.

At the top of a long hike, people often do something odd. They don't look ahead first. They turn around. They look down at the trail, the switchbacks, the parking lot like a toy far below, and someone says it: we came from all the way down there? Their legs remember every step, but it's only from the top that they can see the whole path at once. That's where you are. Today: the first mountain, from the top.
screen: `THE TOP OF A LONG HIKE.` → `THEY TURN AROUND FIRST.` → `WE CAME FROM DOWN THERE?`

segments.voice: Here's the whole year in one sitting. It started with twenty-one words, from metta to the Dhammapada: the vocabulary of the path, one a day. Then the stories. A white elephant in a dream. A birth in a grove. Four sights, a night ride, cut hair. Six hard years, a bowl of rice, a seat under a tree, and dawn. The Deer Park, the growing community, the hard stories, and the sal trees. The Jataka lives, hares and deer and a generous prince. Then the practices: metta, the breath, the walking lane, the refuges and precepts, giving, the chant and the shrine, the holy days, the retreat. Then a whole book, the Dhammapada, read verse by verse. Then the depths: the four rooms, the direct path, the Heart Sutra, the koans, the elders, and the diamond vehicle. Three hundred thirty days. Not all of them were good days. Some you rushed. Some you missed, and came back. The path counted the coming back, not the perfect days. There's a teaching the Buddha gave about a raft. A man reaches a wide river, builds a raft of grass and branches, and paddles across. On the far shore, should he carry the raft on his head for the rest of his journey? No, the Buddha says. The teaching is for crossing, not for carrying around. So from the top, look back with gladness, the mudita you learned for others, turned for once toward yourself. Not pride. Not a scoreboard. Just the plain view of how far you've come. Look how far.
screen: `TWENTY-ONE WORDS, THEN THE STORIES.` · `THE PRACTICES, THEN A WHOLE BOOK.` · `THE DEPTHS.` · `THE RAFT IS FOR CROSSING.` · then, large: `LOOK HOW FAR.`

segments.voice: Today, if you can, sit longer: up to twenty minutes, then rest. The bell holds two; if you have more time, keep sitting after it rings. Let the year pass through your mind, not in order, just whatever surfaces: a word, a story, a verse, a morning you almost skipped. Let each one come and go. When the sit ends, don't jump up. Lean back, or lie down for a minute, and rest at the top. The bell holds the time.
The first mountain. Words, stories, practices, a book and the depths: a whole year of the path, seen at once from the top.
Your line: look how far. Today, tell one person, or just yourself, one way this year has changed how you meet an ordinary day. Day three hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 330 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: YEAR ONE CLOSE: THE BIG LOOKOUT.`

options: carry it on your head, out of gratitude.
fork.reveal: in the parable, the teaching is like a raft: for crossing over, not for holding on to.

trapdoor: what you thought: the top means you're finished.
what it means: the top is where you finally see the whole path at once, and rest before the next one.
what a scholar hears: the raft parable (MN 22, Alagaddupama Sutta) ends with the Buddha saying even good teachings are to be let go of, let alone bad ones.

331.title: Year one close: the big lookout
331.hook: ahead: the Buddha's words in order, the great stories and teachers, the schools, the sources
331.howItsDone: Many Buddhists mark the end of a year or a retreat by resting in quiet sitting, recalling the teachings they have received, and renewing the three refuges before setting out again.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first mountain, from the top, and your line, look how far. Did you let yourself see the distance, just for a moment, without rushing past it? Day three hundred thirty-one.

Three hundred thirty-one days ago, this path began with one word, metta, and one breath. Today is the last day of year one. On a trail, a lookout isn't the summit. It's a ledge with a railing and maybe a bench, where the view opens both ways at once: the climb behind, and in front, ridge after ridge, blue and far away, more mountains than the map seemed to promise. Yesterday was for the view back. Today is a lookout: one glance back, and then a long look ahead.
screen: `DAY ONE: ONE WORD, ONE BREATH.` → `A LEDGE THAT LOOKS BOTH WAYS.` → `RIDGE AFTER RIDGE AHEAD.`

segments.voice: First, the glance back, and only a glance, since yesterday took the long view: five camps, from first words through the stories, the practices and the Dhammapada to the depths. Now turn around. There's a story in the Connected Discourses. The Buddha is staying in a grove of simsapa trees. He picks up a few leaves and asks the monks: which are more, the leaves in my hand, or the leaves in the forest? The forest, of course, they say. Just so, he tells them. What he has come to know is like the forest. What he has taught is like the handful. Why only a handful? Because the handful is what helps: suffering, its cause, its ending, and the way to its ending. So both things are true at once. There's always more, and the handful is enough to walk with. Here's the forest ahead. Year two is the Buddha's own words: the four truths and the eightfold path in depth, then the discourses read in order. Year three is the great story and the teachers: the Buddha's life as a poem, the first disciples and their songs, and the teaching's long journey across Asia. Year four is the schools, each explained in its own terms and never ranked: Theravada thought, the Mahayana sutras, Zen, Pure Land, the Tibetan traditions. Year five is the sources, a little Pali, and a life of practice. And the road itself? In Rhys Davids's translation of the Buddha's last words: "Decay is inherent in all component things! Work out your salvation with diligence!" Everything made will change, this year included. Keep going, and keep going carefully.
screen: `ONE GLANCE BACK AT FIVE CAMPS.` · `A HANDFUL OF LEAVES, A WHOLE FOREST.` · `FOUR YEARS AHEAD.` · `WORK OUT YOUR SALVATION WITH DILIGENCE.` · then, large: `THERE'S ALWAYS MORE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to rest, and look out. Sit comfortably. Let your eyes find the farthest thing you can see: a window, the sky, a wall across the room. That's your lookout. Breathe. Let the year drift past like a landscape: a face, a story, a verse, a hard day you sat through anyway. Don't hold on to any of it. Then let your eyes soften, and simply rest. Nothing to fix. Nothing to finish. If you take refuge, you can say the three refuges silently, once. The bell holds the time.
Year one close. The last day of the first year: a lookout, with the whole climb behind you and ridge after ridge ahead.
Your line: there's always more. Today, notice one leaf, on a tree, on the sidewalk, in a pot on the sill, and let it stand for the handful you carry into year two. Day three hundred thirty-one.

332.title: The elephant's footprint
332.hook: as every footprint fits inside an elephant's, every good teaching fits inside the four truths (MN 28)
332.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in different schools present the four noble truths as a frame for the rest of the teaching, and they are often recited in short form at the start of a talk or retreat.

segments.voice: Yesterday: year one close, and your line, there's always more. Did you find a leaf to stand for the handful you carry? Year two starts now. Day three hundred thirty-two.

Mud after rain, on a forest track in northern India. A deer has crossed here, and a jackal, and a wild boar, and something small with claws. Their prints are everywhere, crisscrossing. And then, right in the middle, one print so wide that you could set every other print inside it with room to spare. An elephant came this way. Year two of the path is called the Buddha's own words, and it begins with that footprint. It isn't the Buddha who points to it, though. It's one of his chief students, standing up before the monks to explain how everything fits together.
screen: `MUD AFTER RAIN.` → `A DEER, A JACKAL, A BOAR.` → `ONE PRINT HOLDS THEM ALL.`

segments.voice: The student is Sariputta, the monk tradition remembers for his wisdom. The talk is number twenty-eight in the Middle-Length Discourses, and its name means the great simile of the elephant's footprint. Sariputta tells the monks: just as the footprints of every creature that walks will fit inside an elephant's footprint, which is the biggest of them all, so every good and wholesome teaching fits inside the four noble truths. Then he names them. The truth of dukkha, the pain and unsatisfactoriness of life. The truth of where it comes from. The truth that it can end. The truth of the way that leads there. You met all four in year one. Here's the surprise. Sariputta doesn't then wander off into lofty ideas. He spends most of the talk on the first truth, and he gets very ordinary about it: your body, made of earth, water, fire and air; the hair, the bones, the breath. He even talks about being insulted and hit, and how to stay steady. In other words, the biggest footprint isn't somewhere far off. It runs right through a regular day. That's the plan for the next three weeks. Each truth, one at a time, in the Buddha's own words where we have them. Then the jobs the Buddha gave each truth, then the chain of causes that sits underneath them. Whatever you learn about generosity, kindness, meditation or ethics later, the claim of this sutta is that it's already inside this one print.
screen: `SARIPUTTA'S GREAT SIMILE.` · `EVERY PRINT FITS INSIDE.` · `FOUR TRUTHS, NAMED AGAIN.` · `THE PRINT RUNS THROUGH A DAY.` · then, large: `THE BIGGEST FOOTPRINT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to recall the four truths. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. On one breath, think: there is dukkha. On the next: it has a cause. Then: it can end. Then: there is a way. Go around the four slowly, one per breath, like stepping into four prints in the mud. If your mind wanders, start again at the first. Nothing to solve. Just walking the outline of the footprint. The bell holds the time.
The elephant's footprint. Sariputta's image for the four noble truths: the one print large enough to hold every other good teaching.
Your line: the biggest footprint. Today, when you notice something that bothers you, see if it fits inside the first truth: there is dukkha. Just notice the fit. Day three hundred thirty-two.

333.title: A physician's pattern
333.hook: later teachers note the truths follow a doctor's steps: illness, cause, cure, treatment
333.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers in many schools present the four truths in the doctor's order, and in Mahayana lands many people pray to or chant the name of the Medicine Buddha for healing of body and mind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the elephant's footprint, and your line, the biggest footprint. Did something that bothered you fit inside the first truth? Day three hundred thirty-three.

A good doctor's visit goes in an order. First: where does it hurt? Then: why might it hurt? Then, the sentence you're waiting for: this can get better. And last: here's what we'll do. Skip a step and things go wrong. Treatment before diagnosis is guessing. A diagnosis with no hope of cure is just bad news. Buddhist teachers noticed long ago that the four noble truths walk in exactly this order. Today, the four truths as a visit to the doctor.
screen: `WHERE DOES IT HURT?` → `WHY?` → `IT CAN GET BETTER.` → `HERE'S WHAT WE'LL DO.`

segments.voice: The pattern goes like this. The first truth, dukkha, is the illness: the ache in life that won't quite go away. The second truth, its arising, is the cause, the thing underneath the symptoms. The third, its ending, is the good news that a cure exists. And the fourth, the path, is the treatment plan. The Buddha's first sermon doesn't use the word doctor. It's later teachers who spell the comparison out. Buddhaghosa, the great fifth-century commentator in Sri Lanka, lays it side by side in his book The Path of Purification: the truth of suffering like a disease, its origin like the cause of the disease, its ending like the cure, the path like the medicine. Teachers in other schools, writing in Sanskrit, use the same picture. And there's an older seed. In a short text called the Itivuttaka, the Buddha describes himself as an unsurpassed physician and surgeon. Over the centuries Buddhists have called him the great physician, and in Mahayana lands a whole Buddha, the Medicine Buddha, carries the image. Some scholars have suggested the four truths borrowed their shape from ancient Indian medicine. Others say the evidence is thin. The sources don't settle it. What the pattern does settle is the order. The Buddha starts with the illness, not the cure. That isn't pessimism. A doctor who says you're sick isn't being gloomy; she's taking you seriously. And the visit doesn't end with the diagnosis. Three of the four truths are about what to do next.
screen: `ILLNESS, CAUSE, CURE, TREATMENT.` · `BUDDHAGHOSA LAYS IT SIDE BY SIDE.` · `A PHYSICIAN AND SURGEON.` · `STARTING WITH THE ILLNESS ISN'T GLOOM.` · then, large: `DIAGNOSE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to name one problem this way. Sit, and let a small, ordinary problem come to mind: a tense conversation, a habit, a worry. Don't fix it. First, just name the hurt, plainly, the way you'd tell a doctor. Breathe. Then ask, gently: what's feeding it? Breathe. Then let yourself consider that it could ease. Breathe. And then, only if something comes, one small step. If nothing comes, the first step was enough. The bell holds the time.
A physician's pattern. The four truths in a doctor's order: illness, cause, cure, and treatment, a comparison later teachers made explicit.
Your line: diagnose first. Today, when something goes wrong, before you reach for the fix, take one breath to name exactly what hurts. Day three hundred thirty-three.

334.title: The first truth, in full
334.hook: birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, not getting what you want: this is dukkha (SN 56.11)
334.howItsDone: In Theravada communities the first sermon is often chanted on Asalha Puja, the full moon that tradition says marks it, and the first truth's list is chanted in Pali.

segments.voice: Yesterday: a physician's pattern, and your line, diagnose first. Did you name what hurt before reaching for the fix? Today, the diagnosis itself. Day three hundred thirty-four.

Late at night, a quiet thought can slip in: everyone else seems to have this figured out. Their parents aren't getting old. Their bodies don't ache. They didn't just lose someone, or miss out on the thing they wanted. Scroll long enough and the feeling hardens into a fact. In a deer park outside Varanasi, the Buddha's first sermon answered that thought with a list. Not a list of your problems. A list of everyone's. Today, the first noble truth, word for word.
screen: `EVERYONE ELSE HAS IT FIGURED OUT.` → `A DEER PARK OUTSIDE VARANASI.` → `A LIST OF EVERYONE'S.`

segments.voice: The sermon is the Turning of the Wheel of the Dhamma, number eleven in the fifty-sixth book of the Connected Discourses. Five former companions are listening. After the middle way, the Buddha names the first truth. In Rhys Davids's old translation it begins: "Birth is attended with pain, decay is painful, disease is painful, death is painful." Then the list keeps going: being joined to what you dislike is painful, being parted from what you love is painful, and not getting what you want is painful. In some versions of the teaching, sorrow, lament, grief and despair are named too. And then a summary line: in short, the five heaps that make up a person, body, feeling, perception, mental formations and consciousness, when they're clung to, are dukkha. Look at what's on the list. Nothing exotic. Nothing that happens only to the unlucky, or the unwise, or people who did something wrong. Birth, aging, getting sick and dying happen to kings and to beggars. Not getting what you want happens to everyone, every day, usually before lunch. So the first truth is general. The Buddha isn't diagnosing you. He's diagnosing being human. And notice the word he uses is dukkha, which English translators have rendered many ways: pain, suffering, ill, unsatisfactoriness, stress. It's a wide word, covering the funeral and the stubbed toe and the long wait in a hospital corridor. The list says: all of this is real, and none of it means you're failing.
screen: `THE TURNING OF THE WHEEL.` · `BIRTH, AGING, SICKNESS, DEATH.` · `NOT GETTING WHAT YOU WANT.` · `A DIAGNOSIS OF BEING HUMAN.` · then, large: `IT'S NOT JUST YOU.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to list today's small dukkhas. Sit, and let your day so far replay at an easy speed. Each time you find a small sting, a late bus, a sore back, a message that didn't come, name it quietly: dukkha. No commentary, no blame. Then, once or twice, let the thought widen: somewhere, right now, someone else has this exact one. Let the breath carry that. The bell holds the time.
The first truth. Birth, aging, sickness, death, being parted from what you love, not getting what you want: this is dukkha, and it belongs to everyone.
Your line: it's not just you. Today, when someone near you is having a hard moment, remember the list, and let it soften how you see them. Day three hundred thirty-four.

335.title: Three kinds of dukkha
335.hook: plain pain, the pain of change, and the unease built into all made things (SN 45.165)
335.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often introduce the three kinds of dukkha when explaining the first truth, and meditators are taught to notice in practice how pleasant feeling, too, changes and passes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the first truth, and your line, it's not just you. Did the list soften how you saw someone having a hard moment? Day three hundred thirty-five.
screen: `THE FIRST TRUTH — IT'S NOT JUST YOU.`

segments.voice: Three moments from one ordinary week. On Monday you slam your finger in a drawer, and for ten seconds the whole world is your finger. On Friday you're on the last evening of a wonderful trip, the sun going down over the water, and right in the middle of the happiness there's a small sinking feeling, because tomorrow it ends. And on Sunday afternoon, with nothing at all wrong, there's a faint restlessness you can't name. All three are dukkha. But they aren't the same kind. Today, a short sutta that sorts them.
screen: `MONDAY: A FINGER IN A DRAWER.` → `FRIDAY: THE LAST EVENING.` → `SUNDAY: A RESTLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: The sutta is tiny, number one hundred sixty-five in the book on the path in the Connected Discourses. The Buddha says there are three kinds of dukkha, and names them. The first is dukkha as plain pain: the finger in the drawer, the headache, the grief. Nobody needs this one explained. The second is dukkha as change. This is the strange one, because it lives inside pleasant things. The trip is lovely, and because it's lovely its ending hurts. Every good thing comes with its end built in. The commentaries say pleasant feeling counts here: not because pleasure is bad, but because it doesn't stay. The third is harder to spot: the dukkha of formations, of all conditioned things. Everything that's made out of parts, and depends on other things, is unstable. Your body, your plans, your mood, the economy. On this reading, even a quiet Sunday with nothing wrong rests on ground that isn't solid. That background unease is the third kind. The sutta itself is very short; the full explanations come from the commentaries, and teachers draw the lines between the three a little differently. Here's why the sorting helps. If all you know is the first kind, you'll think dukkha is only bad luck. The second kind explains why getting what you wanted didn't settle you. The third explains Sunday afternoon. And the sutta's last sentence ties it to the path: the eightfold path, the Buddha says, is to be developed for fully understanding these three.
screen: `PLAIN PAIN.` · `THE PAIN OF CHANGE.` · `THE UNEASE OF MADE THINGS.` · `THE PATH IS FOR UNDERSTANDING THEM.` · then, large: `THREE KINDS.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to spot each kind once. Sit and breathe. First, find any plain discomfort in the body right now: a tight shoulder, a sore spot. Name it: pain. Then think of something pleasant you're looking forward to, and notice whether there's a tiny edge of worry that it'll end. Name it: change. Then, for a few breaths, just feel the whole moment, made of a hundred moving parts. If there's a faint unease underneath, name it: made things. The bell holds the time.
Three kinds of dukkha. Plain pain, the pain of change hidden inside pleasant things, and the quiet unease built into everything made of parts.
Your line: three kinds. Today, when something feels off, ask which kind it is: pain, change, or the ground moving under made things. Day three hundred thirty-five.

original.note: Pali dukkhatā: the state of being dukkha; the sutta names three, from pain, from change, and from formations.

336.title: To be understood
336.hook: the first truth's task is to be understood, not fixed or blamed (SN 56.11)
336.howItsDone: In meditation, many Buddhists are taught to turn toward discomfort and investigate it, noting where it is and how it changes, rather than reacting to it at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three kinds of dukkha, and your line, three kinds. Did you catch pain, change, or the quiet unease of made things? Today ends the first week of year two. Day three hundred thirty-six.

When something hurts, there are two buttons within easy reach. The first says fix it: take something, buy something, change the plan, make it stop. The second says blame it: whose fault is this, mine or theirs? Both buttons are fast. Both feel like doing something. In the first sermon, the Buddha gives the first truth a job, and it isn't either button. He says this truth is to be understood. Today, what that single word asks of us, and a look back at the week.
screen: `BUTTON ONE: FIX IT.` → `BUTTON TWO: BLAME IT.` → `A THIRD JOB.`

segments.voice: In the first sermon, each truth comes with a task. Over the coming week we'll meet the other three. The first truth's task, in Pali, is pariññeyya: to be fully understood, known all the way around. Pali dictionaries read pari as around or fully, joined to the verb to know. Picture walking all the way around a boulder that's fallen across your path, looking at it from every side, before you try to move it. Notice what the Buddha doesn't say. He doesn't say dukkha is to be fixed. The sermon gives the job of letting go to the second truth, the cause, not to the pain itself. He doesn't say it's to be blamed, on you or anyone. He doesn't say ignore it, either. He says understand it. That changes how a bad moment feels from the inside. A pain you're fighting has two parts: the pain, and the fight. A pain you're studying, gently, with curiosity, has a little room around it. So here's the week, looked at from the top. It opened with the elephant's footprint, Sariputta's picture of the four truths holding every good teaching. Then a physician's pattern: illness, cause, cure, treatment. Then the first truth in full: birth, aging, sickness, death, not getting what you want. Then three kinds of dukkha: pain, change, and the unease of made things. And today: what to do with all of it. Not fix, not blame. Understand.
screen: `EACH TRUTH HAS A TASK.` · `PARIÑÑEYYA: KNOWN ALL THE WAY AROUND.` · `NOT FIXED, NOT BLAMED.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `UNDERSTAND IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to understand one pain. Sit and settle. Choose one small pain, in the body or the heart. Don't push it away and don't ask whose fault it is. Walk around it. Where exactly is it? Is it sharp, dull, heavy, hot? Does it stay the same, or shift from breath to breath? What thoughts gather around it? Just look, the way you'd study a stone in your hand. If it gets too much, come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
To be understood. The first truth's task in the first sermon: dukkha is to be fully known, all the way around, not fixed in a hurry or blamed.
Your line: understand it. Today, when you feel your hand reaching for the fix-it button or the blame button, pause, and ask one question about the pain first. Day three hundred thirty-six.
